Defensive id Parsing

A non-numeric id used to just fail to match; against Prisma it throws — so it needs its own check.

Lesson 1's getTicketById converted req.params.id with Number(...) and handed it straight to Array.find() — a non-numeric id like /tickets/abc became NaN, find() simply never matched anything, and the existing "not found" branch handled it fine by accident. Prisma is less forgiving about it: findUnique({ where: { id: NaN } }) doesn't return "not found," it throws, because NaN isn't a value the id column can hold at all — and an uncaught throw from an async controller becomes a 500 through asyncHandler and the centralized error handler (Lesson 1), not the 400 a malformed request actually deserves.

// Figure 2.16: guarding against a bad id (src/controllers/ticket.controller.js, excerpt)
export const getTicketById = asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const id = Number(req.params.id);

  if (Number.isNaN(id)) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: { message: 'id must be a number' } });
  }

  const ticket = await ticketService.getTicketById(id);
  // ...unchanged from Lesson 1 from here
});

Number.isNaN(id) catches exactly that case, before ticketService — and therefore Prisma — ever sees it, turning what would otherwise be a confusing 500 into a 400 that actually names the problem. It's the same "plain manual check, fail with a clear message" habit as every other validation in this project so far — a schema-based version arrives with Zod in Week 3, but the underlying reason to check at all doesn't change: swapping the store underneath a service can expose gaps in validation that happened to be harmless against the old, more forgiving implementation.
